title: Network Basics — ip, ss, DNS, Ports
lead: Read your network identity: address, gateway, port and name. Almost every command in this module is read-only.
objectives: You read the IP address, prefix and default gateway with `ip a` and `ip r`.
You see which service listens on which port and interface with `ss -tulpn`.
You know the name resolution chain: `/etc/hosts` → `/etc/resolv.conf` → DNS server.
You read the firewall (firewalld / ufw) first and change it without locking yourself out.
You diagnose "no internet" layer by layer (address → gateway → IP → name).

sections.title: Address and routing: ip a, ip r
body: Every network interface (`eth0`, `ens3`, `enp0s3`, `lo`) has an **IP address** and a **prefix**. `192.168.1.42/24` means: the first 24 bits are the network, the rest identifies the host (`/24` = `255.255.255.0`). `lo` is the loopback interface (`127.0.0.1`): the machine itself, it never leaves the host.

If the destination is not on the local network, the packet goes to the **default gateway**. The line `default via 192.168.1.1` in `ip r` tells you which. Use the modern `ip` command instead of the old `ifconfig` and `route`; it exists on Rocky/Alma and Ubuntu/Debian alike.
Interface names vary by distribution and VM; your output may show `ens3` or `enp0s3` instead of `eth0`.

commands.what: Lists all interfaces with their IP addresses and state (UP/DOWN).
commands.where: To learn the machine's address or verify an interface is up.
commands.why: First stop in network trouble; without an address nothing above it works.

commands.what: Shows the same information as a short one-line-per-interface table.
commands.where: For a quick look at which interface has which address.
commands.why: Saves you from reading long output; it fits on the screen.

commands.what: Shows the routing table; the `default via` line is the gateway.
commands.where: When investigating why you cannot reach outside networks.
commands.why: Without a default route no packet leaves the local network.

commands.what: Filters lines by text; here it finds the gateway in saved route output.
commands.where: When you want a single line out of long output.
commands.why: The same filtering works on `ss` output; in the simulator you practise with sample files.

sections.tip: Chain it with cutting: `grep default ~/net/routes.txt | cut -d' ' -f3` returns just the gateway address.
sections.warn: Changing an interface address by hand with `ip addr add/del` can cut your connection (including SSH) instantly. In this module we only read.

sections.title: Ports and listening services: ss
body: The IP address selects the machine, the **port** selects the service on it: `22` SSH, `80` HTTP, `443` HTTPS, `53` DNS. A running service **listens** (LISTEN) on a specific address and port.
`ss -tulpn` letters: `t` TCP, `u` UDP, `l` listening only, `p` process name, `n` numeric output (no name lookup). You need `sudo` to see process names.

**Watch the local address:** `0.0.0.0:22` means reachable on every interface. `127.0.0.1:5432` is reachable only from the machine itself. A database listening on `0.0.0.0` may be exposed to the network, which is a security finding.
`ss` replaced the old `netstat -tulpn`; the options are nearly the same.

commands.what: Lists listening TCP/UDP sockets with ports and processes.
commands.where: To answer "is the service really listening, and on which address?"
commands.why: A service may look running yet listen on the wrong address, so connections fail.

commands.what: Shows only TCP listeners, without process info (no sudo needed).
commands.where: For quick checks or in scripts.
commands.why: Short and unprivileged; enough to see whether a port is open.

commands.what: Fetches only the response headers of a web server.
commands.where: To test whether the service really answers over HTTP.
commands.why: A port can be open while the application does not answer; a code like `200` or `301` shows it does.

sections.tip: Filter `ss` output: `ss -tln | grep LISTEN | wc -l` counts how many TCP ports listen.
sections.warn: Do not port-scan servers you do not own. It is unethical and noticeable; work on `127.0.0.1` of your own VM.

sections.title: Name resolution: hosts, resolv.conf, DNS
body: A name (`example.com`) is turned into an IP in this order: first `/etc/hosts` is checked, then the **DNS server** listed in `/etc/resolv.conf` is asked (the order is set by the `hosts:` line in `/etc/nsswitch.conf`).
`/etc/hosts` holds local, hand-written mappings: `192.168.1.50 intranet.lab`. Great for tests, but it only affects that machine.

`/etc/resolv.conf` is usually generated by NetworkManager or systemd-resolved; hand edits can be overwritten on reboot. On Ubuntu you often see `127.0.0.53` in it; `resolvectl status` shows the real server.
**Key distinction:** if `ping 1.1.1.1` works but `ping example.com` does not, your network is fine and the problem is DNS.

commands.where: When a name goes to an unexpected address.
commands.why: `/etc/hosts` is read before DNS; a wrong line overrides all resolution.

commands.what: Shows the DNS servers (`nameserver`) and search domain (`search`) in use.
commands.where: First file to check when names do not resolve.
commands.why: A wrong or unreachable `nameserver` line breaks all name resolution.

commands.what: Resolves a name the way the system really does (hosts + DNS).
commands.where: To test what applications will see.
commands.why: It also honours `/etc/hosts`, so it is more accurate than tools that only query DNS.

commands.what: Shows per-interface DNS servers on systemd-resolved systems.
commands.where: On Ubuntu and newer Rocky/Alma when `resolv.conf` does not tell enough.
commands.why: Reveals the real DNS server behind `127.0.0.53`.

sections.warn: One wrong `nameserver` line breaks all name resolution. On a production machine configure DNS via NetworkManager (`nmcli`) or netplan instead of editing `/etc/resolv.conf`.

sections.title: Firewall: firewalld and ufw
body: Even if a service listens, the **firewall** may block the port. Rocky/Alma/RHEL use `firewalld` (`firewall-cmd`), Ubuntu/Debian use `ufw`.

In firewalld changes are **runtime** by default: effective immediately but lost on reload or reboot. To make them permanent add `--permanent` and run `--reload`. ufw rules are permanent automatically.
**Read** first: `firewall-cmd --list-all` or `ufw status verbose`. Then change.
SELinux (Rocky) and AppArmor (Ubuntu) are a separate layer; opening the port does not always mean the service may use it, but that is outside this module.

commands.what: Shows allowed services and ports of the active zone.
commands.where: On Rocky/Alma/RHEL when a port is not reachable from outside.
commands.why: You see at a glance which services or ports are allowed; read-only and safe.

commands.what: Opens a port; without `--permanent` it is runtime only.
commands.where: When you must expose a service to the outside.
commands.why: Try at runtime first and make permanent once it works; mistakes disappear with a reload.

commands.what: Shows the firewall state and rules on Ubuntu/Debian.
commands.where: When auditing rules on an Ubuntu server.
commands.why: `inactive` means the firewall is off; `active` shows the default policy.

sections.tip: On Rocky a rule added with `--timeout=300` disappears after 5 minutes; if you make a mistake it heals itself.
sections.warn: When changing the firewall over SSH keep a second SSH session open and use `--timeout` first. Before `ufw enable` allow SSH with `sudo ufw allow 22/tcp`.
sections.danger: Applying a rule remotely that closes the SSH port or sets the default policy to `deny` locks you out. Take a VM snapshot first (module 0.2) and keep console access ready.

sections.title: Diagnosis ladder: bottom to top
body: Solve "no internet" **layer by layer**; the first failing step is where the problem is: (1) is the interface UP with an address? (2) does a ping to the gateway work? (3) does a ping to an outside IP (`1.1.1.1`) work? (4) does the name resolve? (5) does the service listen and does the firewall allow it?
`ping` uses ICMP; some networks block ICMP, so a failed ping does not always mean no connectivity. Also try the real service with `curl -I`.
Constant `ping` needlessly burdens the target; limit the count with `-c 3`.

commands.what: Sends 3 ICMP packets to the target and measures the reply time.
commands.where: To test gateway, outside IP and name separately.
commands.why: Shows which layer is broken, one at a time.

commands.what: Splits a line into fields by a delimiter and takes the field you want.
commands.where: To pull one value such as address, port or prefix out of output.
commands.why: You pass the value into a file or the next command without copying by hand.

commands.what: Sorts lines numerically and removes duplicates.
commands.where: When producing a clean list of listening ports.
commands.why: Gives a tidy, duplicate-free list for reports and comparison.

sections.tip: Write your findings into a report: `hostname > ~/net/report.txt`, then append with `>>`. It makes pasting into a support ticket easy.

t01.text: Read the sample route file: `cat ~/net/routes.txt`. Which line names the gateway?

t02.text: Show only the listening (LISTEN) lines of `~/net/ss.txt`.

t03.text: Read the local name mappings with `cat /etc/hosts`.

t04.text: Find the default route with `grep default ~/net/routes.txt`. What is the gateway address?

t05.text: Write only the gateway address into `~/net/gateway.txt`.
t05.hint: `grep default ... | cut -d' ' -f3 > ~/net/gateway.txt`; field 3 is the gateway.

t06.text: Write the number of listening (LISTEN) lines into `~/net/listen_count.txt`.
t06.hint: A pipeline like `grep LISTEN ... | wc -l > file`.

t07.text: Write the externally exposed listeners (LISTEN lines that are not `127.0.0.1`) into `~/net/exposed.txt`.
t07.hint: Pipe two `grep`s together; use `-v 127.0.0.1` in the second.

t08.text: Predict: which process listens on port 8080? Then verify with `grep 8080 ~/net/ss.txt`.
t08.hint: Look at the `users:((...))` part at the end of the line.

t09.text: Predict: which address and prefix does `eth0` carry? Verify with `grep 192 ~/net/ipa.txt`.

t10.text: Predict: what does `echo 192.168.1.42/24 | cut -d/ -f2` print? Run it and check.
t10.hint: The field after the `/` character: the prefix length.

t11.text: Debug: the `nameserver` in `~/net/resolv.conf` is invalid. Rewrite the file so it has two lines: `nameserver 192.168.1.1` and `nameserver 1.1.1.1`.
t11.hint: `printf 'line1\nline2\n' > file` writes two lines; look at the error with `cat` first.

t12.text: Debug: the script `~/net/check_ports.sh` does not run. Find the cause, fix it and run the script.

t13.text: Mini report: write the host name, the gateway address and the number of listening services (3 lines, in that order) into `~/net/report.txt`.
t13.hint: Use `>` in the first command and `>>` in the following ones; `hostname` gives the host name.

t14.text: Hard: from the LISTEN lines of `ss.txt` write only the port numbers, numerically sorted and without duplicates, into `~/net/ports.txt` (one port per line).
t14.hint: `grep LISTEN | tr -s ' ' | cut -d' ' -f5 | cut -d: -f2 | sort -n | uniq > file`

t15.text: Hard: write the firewalld plan for opening 8080/tcp permanently into `~/net/fw_plan.txt` as two lines: first the command containing `--permanent --add-port=8080/tcp`, then `firewall-cmd --reload`. (You write the plan, you do not run it.)
t15.hint: `echo 'command' > file`, use `>>` for the second line. Use quotes.

t16.text: Ticket: Users cannot reach the name `intranet.lab`. The internal server's address is `192.168.1.50`. Add this mapping to `~/net/hosts` (do not delete existing lines).

t17.text: Ticket: A security audit wants proof that PostgreSQL (port 5432) listens only on the local address. Save the relevant `ss.txt` line into `~/net/audit.txt`.

vm.intro: These steps run on your own VM and only read. Outputs are specific to you; IPs and interface names may differ. If a command is missing, install `sudo dnf install iproute bind-utils` on Rocky or `sudo apt install iproute2 dnsutils` on Ubuntu.

v01.title: Address and gateway
v01.text: Read your interfaces and route and paste the output.

blocks.expected:
lo      UNKNOWN  127.0.0.1/8
ens3    UP       192.168.1.42/24
default via 192.168.1.1 dev ens3 proto dhcp metric 100
192.168.1.0/24 dev ens3 proto kernel scope link src 192.168.1.42

differs: The interface may be called `eth0`, `ens3` or `enp0s3`; what matters is the address and the `default via` line.
If there is no `default` line the machine has no gateway; check the VM's network mode (NAT/Bridge).

v02.title: Listening services
v02.text: List which services listen and find SSH.

blocks.expected:
Netid State  Local Address:Port Process
tcp   LISTEN 0.0.0.0:22         users:(("sshd",pid=812,fd=3))
...

differs: Without `sudo` the process name (`Process` column) stays empty.
If `ss` is missing install `iproute`/`iproute2`; if there is no `LISTEN` line the service is not running.

v03.title: Name resolution chain
v03.text: Read hosts and resolv.conf, then resolve a name the way the system does.

blocks.cmd:
cat /etc/hosts
cat /etc/resolv.conf
resolvectl status | head -n 15
getent hosts localhost

differs: If `resolvectl` is missing (old or minimal system) skip that line; `resolv.conf` is enough.
Seeing `nameserver 127.0.0.53` on Ubuntu is normal; the real server is listed in `resolvectl status`.

v04.title: Diagnosis ladder
v04.text: Ping the gateway, an outside IP and a name, 2 packets each. Replace `192.168.1.1` with your own gateway.
differs: If the IP answers but the name does not, the problem is DNS (`/etc/resolv.conf`).
If none answer, check address/gateway with `ip a` and `ip r` first; some networks block ICMP, so also try `curl -I https://example.com`.

v05.title: Create your own listener and see it
v05.text: Start a temporary web server on `127.0.0.1` only, see it with `ss`, test it with `curl`, then stop it.

blocks.cmd:
python3 -m http.server 8080 --bind 127.0.0.1 &
sleep 1
ss -tln | grep 8080
curl -I http://127.0.0.1:8080
kill %1

differs: If `python3` is missing it needs installing; you can skip and paste your `ss -tln` output instead.
If the port is busy use `8081`. When done, verify with `jobs` that no background job remains.

v06.title: Read the firewall (do not change it)
v06.text: Read your distribution's firewall state. Add no rule for now. Before changing rules take a VM snapshot (module 0.2) and keep a second SSH session open.

blocks.cmd:
# Rocky / Alma / RHEL
sudo firewall-cmd --state
sudo firewall-cmd --list-all
# Ubuntu / Debian
sudo ufw status verbose
blocks.expected:
running
public (active)
  services: cockpit dhcpv6-client ssh
# or: Status: inactive

differs: The command that does not belong to your distribution prints `command not found`; that is normal, run the other one.
`not running` or `inactive` means the firewall is off; you do not need to change that in this lab.

q1.q: Which command shows the default gateway?
q1.explain: `ip r` shows the routing table; the `default via ...` line is the gateway. `ip a` shows addresses, `ss` listening ports, `/etc/hosts` name mappings.

q2.q: In `ss -tulpn` output a database listens on `127.0.0.1:5432`. Who can connect to it?
options: Only those with a firewall rule
q2.explain: `127.0.0.1` is the loopback address; the service is reachable locally only. Exposed to the outside is `0.0.0.0` or an external interface address.

q3.q: In which order is a name usually resolved?
options: First `/etc/hosts`, then the DNS server in `resolv.conf`
q3.explain: The `hosts:` line in `nsswitch.conf` sets the order; by default the file (`/etc/hosts`) comes first, then DNS.

q4.q: What happens if you run `firewall-cmd --add-port=8080/tcp` without `--permanent`?
options: The rule only applies after a reboot
The rule applies immediately but is lost on reload or reboot
q4.explain: The default is the runtime configuration: effective at once, not persistent. To make it permanent you need `--permanent` and `--reload`.

summary: `ip a` shows addresses, `ip r` the routes and the default gateway.
`ss -tulpn` shows listening services; `127.0.0.1` is local only, `0.0.0.0` is every interface.
Read the firewall first; in firewalld separate runtime from permanent, and over SSH use `--timeout` and a second session.
Diagnosis: address → gateway → outside IP → name → service and firewall.

glossary.meaning: The address of an interface on the network, e.g. 192.168.1.42.
Separates the network and host part of an address; /24 = 255.255.255.0.
The router address to which packets for destinations outside the local network are sent.
A number that selects a service on a machine; 22 SSH, 80 HTTP, 443 HTTPS.
A service waiting for connections on a specific address and port.
The system that translates names into IP addresses.
Temporary (until reload) and persistent configuration in firewalld.
A simple network protocol that measures reachability and latency.
